blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- because an awfully long time has gone by since whenever it was, 10 October. It would be helpful, I think, just to have the framework, knowing that there are essentially four incidents, how they are going to be dealt with, and do it that way.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Good morning, members of the jury. As you know, we're moving on to the next baby, [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm going to invite Mr Johnson very briefly to remind us of what the situation so far as [Baby I] is concerned was because a long time has gone by since you heard the opening of this case and you've heard an awful lot of evidence about a large number of babies now, just so that you can focus on what's going to come by way of evidence in relation to [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you go to your first jury bundle, ladies and gentlemen, at divider 12, so jury bundle -- sorry, divider 1, jury bundle 1. It's page 5. It's the indictment. Page 5, count 12. That's where my confusion arose.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you can see there that there is a single allegation so far as [Baby I] is concerned. The allegation is one of murder. You will remember that the way the indictment is structured is that where there is an event that the prosecution allege is a murder, we haven't broken it down into the individual attempts to murder when the attempts result in the completed offence. That's why although [Baby I]'s case is probably the most factually involved, and probably will take the longest of all these children's cases to present, there is a single count.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are four separate events. So just in a few seconds I'm going to give you a framework that we're going to work to.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was born on 4 August 2015, so putting that in context, about 8 weeks before the events that we were considering yesterday on the 26th and 27 September. She was born in the Liverpool Women's Hospital on 4 August.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was 27 weeks' gestation when born, weighed 960 grams, which is about 2 pounds and 2 ounces, and she was transferred to the Countess of Chester on 18 August.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then back to the Liverpool Women's Hospital on 6 September and then back for the second time to Chester on 13 September. The first episode that the prosecution say was of concern, and we say frankly involved Lucy Letby trying to kill [Baby I], was on 30 September.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We'll deal with that episode first.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The second episode was on the night shift of the 12th into 13 October. The third episode was the next night shift, the 13th into 14 October. Following that, [Baby I] was transferred out to Arrowe Park, the tertiary hospital on the Wirral. She returned to Chester 2 days later on 17 October and then you will see, looking at count 12, the date that we say Lucy Letby completed the offence that she'd been attempting over several days, 23 October 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the day she died. In a murder the act causing the death may not occur on the day that the person actually dies. Sometimes it can occur days before. But here, as you've heard Mr Johnson say, there are a number -- four episodes that are going to be considered by the evidence that's going to be adduced and it was after the last episode that [Baby I] died or in the last episode.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. In a nutshell, the case involves air, milk and -- well, air in the stomach and air in the circulation at various stages.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of [MOTHER OF BABY I] (read)
My Lord, may I begin to present the evidence through the reading of statements of [Mother of Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The first of which, members of the jury, is dated 20 July 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am [Mother of Baby I], mother of [Baby I]. I live with my partner [Father of Baby I]. In around April 2015 I found out I was pregnant. All of my scans came back normal.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I had a twelve-week scan at the Countess of Chester Hospital and then I paid privately to have a 16-week scan, which was to determine our baby's sex. We were told we were having a girl.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Then at 21 weeks at the Countess of Chester Hospital we had our last scan. At no time during any of my scans were any concerns raised. My baby was developing as expected. I didn't have any antenatal appointments as I had breezed through my past pregnancies and there were no areas of concern.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Then, five weeks after my last scan, my waters broke. I went to the Countess of Chester Hospital to the labour ward. Initially, they tried to tell me that I could have just leaked, but I knew my waters had broken. It wasn't my first baby and I knew what it felt like when your waters go.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember they conducted some checks, which proved my waters had gone. This resulted in me being transferred that night to the Manchester Royal Hospital by ambulance and [Father of Baby I] following in his car.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I arrived they conducted more blood tests and I was regularly monitored. I was kept there over the weekend. They told us what to expect and if I didn't get an infection they wouldn't leave me past 34 weeks, so no matter what, she would be born prior to 34 weeks. The medical staff kept telling me that she was safer inside me at this time. However, if she was still inside after 34 weeks she would have to be then delivered due the risk of infection.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "By Monday, due to there being no sign of infection, I was sent home with the agreement that I would go to the Countess of Chester every 2 to 3 days to get my bloods checked. However, I only got to the first appointment, which was on the following Wednesday, because when the nurse took my bloods she informed me that I would have to stay in as my blood levels were a bit high and they'd like to keep an eye on me, plus they were waiting for my blood results from Manchester to be sent through so they could compare them to see how much they had risen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After they compared my two sets of results, I was told I couldn't leave as my levels appeared to have shot through the roof. The Countess then transferred me that day, via ambulance, to the Liverpool Women's Hospital. On arrival, I was booked in and given a room on their maternity ward whilst my bloods were checked again.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Over the next few days I was continually monitored. By Friday, 7 August 2015, I received a further scan. From the scan I was informed that there was still some water left and that my baby was still safer in than out. The doctor continued to say that I had become poorly before my baby did, so my blood pressure and temperature were continually monitored.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Later the same day, I remember my kids had come to visit and I was sat with them in the hospital canteen when my back started to ache. I recall telling my sister that she would have to take them home now as it was getting late. I said goodbye to them and [Father of Baby I] asked me if I was coming out to the car to which I informed him that I was in labour and that I needed to get back upstairs to the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I got back on to the maternity ward, a midwife came and I was attached to a monitor. She informed me that I wasn't in labour and then left. I told [Father of Baby I], 'I don't care what the machine says, I'm having contractions, go and get her back'. She returned and gave me a couple of paracetamols and left again, saying I wasn't.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As I wasn't happy, I spoke with a friend of mine, Debbie, who is a midwife at the same hospital. She went and got a male doctor. The doctor instructed the staff to remove me from the monitor and he physically checked me. After his examination, he sent for me to go straight to the labour ward as I was 6 centimetres dilated.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A further midwife and a neonatal team arrived shortly afterwards. During this time my contractions just stopped. I think it was out of fear as I was too scared to push, so the staff checked the monitors and from there they were able to see my contractions and they'd tell me when I needed to push.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At some point they informed me that my baby was getting in distress so I pushed harder and she came out. Our baby, who was named [Baby I], was born at 9.02 pm on the evening of 7 August 2015, weighing 2 pounds 2 ounces. I was only in the labour room for around an hour. I never had any pain relief, nor did I need any intervention.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Prior to [Baby I]'s birth I was informed that she would immediately be removed to the neonatal ward and I would be able to see her later, but when she was born she was doing really well and they actually kept her in the room for a little bit and brought her over to the bed for me to see her and then they took her upstairs. [Father of Baby I] was present during the birth.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I freshened up and went back to the maternity ward, where we had a private room. We then just waited and waited for hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Eventually, a nurse came down and told us as [Baby I] only weighed 2 pounds 2 ounces, they were struggling to get her lines in and that they had to scan her each time to see if the line had been inserted correctly and on a number of occasions it hadn't been.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At around 3 am we were allowed to see her for around 10 to 15 minutes. She was in an incubator on a ventilator. The ratio at Liverpool Women's was one nurse to two babies. [Baby I] was covered in a sterile tissue-like cover as they didn't want her to get an infection from where they had entered or attempted to secure her lines.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We then returned back to the maternity ward and both stayed over. The following morning at around 06.30 hours, [Father of Baby I] and I went back up to see [Baby I]. She was still on the neonatal ward, room 7. She was still in an incubator. She wasn't on a ventilator, she just had a BiPAP mask.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A nurse told us that this was due to the fact that [Baby I] had fought the ventilator, so they removed it and placed the BiPAP mask on instead. One of the nurses then asked if we'd like to get her out. At first we were reluctant, but they confirmed that it would be okay. However, as soon as [Baby I] was placed on to my chest, her saturation levels dropped, so she was put back into the incubator where her levels improved. The nursing staff said that it might have just been a bit too soon to remove her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] appeared fine whilst in the incubator as she was kicking and her hands were going everywhere and it was just us that were scared to touch her. During that day [Father of Baby I] and I were spoken to by one of the male neonatal doctors and informed about what to expect. We were told [Baby I] would likely be with them for a long time, but she was doing really, really well, and that there were no complications and the next week would indicate which way it was going to go for her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On hearing this, I was initially petrified as I didn't know if she was going to come through, but she was fine and eventually all of my fear just went away. [Baby I] was just small. The nurses kept telling me that I must have really looked after myself for her to come out as she had. I could see other babies on the ward that had been born of a similar age to [Baby I] and they were struggling but [Baby I] wasn't.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After a few days, [Baby I] was taken off the CPAP. I was told she was sitting fine on the machine and she wasn't being tired out, so they were going to put her on 4 hours of oxygen, followed by 4 hours off. I initially raised some concerns, but they said she was healthy enough to do it the old-fashioned way. So they did that for a couple of days and it was again all good
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: news. She didn't actually need the oxygen all of the time, so we were really positive at this point.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby I] was approximately 5 days old we were told that [Baby I] was going to be moved into room 2 on the neonatal intensive care unit, which is not an intensive care unit, it's more like a high dependency unit. We thought that was brilliant news.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "However, the next day, a further doctor came in and said [Baby I] didn't need to be at Liverpool Women's anymore and she's going to be transferred back to Chester. On hearing this, we initially panicked as we didn't want her to go back. Liverpool Women's was spotless, the floors shone, and [Baby I] was settled there. But again they said [Baby I] didn't need to be there anymore.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At around the same time we had also heard that a virus had broken out on ward 2 in Liverpool, so on hearing this, I agreed for [Baby I] be moved back to Chester to reduce the risk of her catching anything.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 18 August [Baby I] was transferred back to Chester by ambulance."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then describes where [Baby I] went to, saying:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The neonatal ward is located at the rear of the hospital by the maternity ward. It has four separate rooms, numbered 1 to 4. Each room cares for babies who need separate levels of care and were at different levels of help."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She defines room 1 as the intensive care room and that it could accommodate up to eight babies with a ratio of one nurse to four babies:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was placed into room 1. At first, I had reservations about [Baby I]'s care. I felt they didn't have time for [Baby I]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then refers to a nurse by the name of Bernie, and you, members of the jury, will shortly hear evidence in relation to Nurse Bernadette Butterworth.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Returning to [Mother of Baby I]'s statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bernie had her, but they were so busy. I remember on one occasion we asked if we could get her out of the incubator but Bernie told us no as she didn't have the time to do it. I remember saying to my mum, 'I don't want her here [meaning [Baby I]], they're not giving her enough time'. I also queried [Baby
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I]'s oxygen intake as they kept putting her on oxygen if her stats dropped lower than 96. I had heard previously that too much oxygen was bad for babies, so I wasn't very happy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Then a couple of days later, [Dr B] came and informed us that [Baby I] had had a scan and, from this scan, they could see that she'd had a small bleed on her brain. The doctor then went on to say that this could have been caused by lack of or too much oxygen. I felt that Chester and Liverpool had different methods, as Chester were more concerned about feeding and growing as opposed to Liverpool Women's, who wanted to get the babies off oxygen. They just had different methods and over time the nurses would explain why they were doing certain things.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I also remember [Baby I] continued to wear a CPAP mask. The problem was it was too big for her face. Staff at the hospital used cotton buds to try and pad it out, but this just caused her face to mark and dint. I remember going home one night and asking Jo, who was another senior nurse, full name not known, if she could please just lift it or move it slightly as it was marking [Baby I]'s face. The following day, when we returned, [Baby I] no longer had it on and I was informed that she didn't need it anymore. I remember feeling annoyed because if she didn't need it, why hadn't they thought to remove it and prevent [Baby I] having these marks prior to me asking?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby I] was around 2 weeks old, she was moved to room 2 and it was good in there. I met other families, one of them being [Mother of Baby G], whose daughter [Baby G] had also been born prematurely at 23 weeks, but she was now 3 months.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst in room 2, [Baby I] received her first bottle. A nurse called Nicky came in and I remember Nicky was sneezing and coughing whilst putting her hands in [Baby I]'s incubator. I was fuming, absolutely fuming, because we were doing everything to stop [Baby I] from getting an infection. I was so annoyed that I had to go outside and phone the nursing desk and tell them that under no circumstances was anyone with a cold or a cough to come near my daughter. I had to phone them because if I'd seen someone, I would have lost it. And to top it off, whilst Nicky was in the room, the doctor, who was seeing another baby, asked Nicky if she was full of a cold, to which she said, 'Yeah, I've been full of it for days'. So even the doctors were aware and didn't do anything.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After I had calmed down, I helped give [Baby I] her bottle, which she took well. [Baby I] was then placed back into the incubator. Near to the end of the nurses' shift, [Father of Baby I] asked if he could hold [Baby I], to which Bernie agreed, but said it could only be for 10 minutes as they were changing over staff. This again annoyed me because had he waited a further 30
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: minutes, when the staff changed over to the night block, we could have held her for a couple of hours instead of just 10 minutes. This was due to the fact that they limited [Baby I]'s movements and now that [Father of Baby I] had moved her we wouldn't be able to hold her again for some time, so I left the ward.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I returned, [Baby I]'s stats had dropped, so either the morning or night nurses had called for the doctor. Dr Matt arrived [as read]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, members of the jury, you heard evidence from a Dr Matthew Neame a day or two ago and you'll hear evidence again from him in relation to this count.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Returning to the statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Matt arrived and I recognised him as he'd previously looked after [Baby I] when she was in room 7 at the Liverpool Women's. I was so relieved it was someone we knew. He's not actually called Dr Matt, we just called him that because we knew his first name was Matt. Dr Matt informed us that she needed a little help breathing so he had put her on high flow. He then conducted a lumbar puncture to check her bloods, just to see if she was picking anything up.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby I]'s stats had settled, Dr Matt returned back to the other ward. However, when we arrived home that evening, we received a phone call asking us to go back in as they had had to put [Baby I] on a ventilator due to her becoming poorly again. The following day, [Baby I] was returned back to Liverpool Women's. She was 4 weeks old and this was the start of her becoming poorly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Initially, Chester told us that they suspected [Baby I] had NEC, necrotising enterocolitis, because her stomach had swelled and her veins were visible. We were also informed that she needed to go to Liverpool so she was close to Alder Hey in case -- to be near to Alder Hey -- bowel rupture and they needed to operate [as read]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It must mean in case she needed surgery at Alder Hey, that being the surgical centre as you already know. Returning to [Mother of Baby I]'s statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "But when we arrived, Liverpool said that [Baby I] didn't have NEC and within 24 hours she'd gone from being fully ventilated at Chester to no ventilation and starting back on feeds. [Baby I] remained at Liverpool for a further week. During this time they never checked [Baby I]'s bowel and I think if they had just
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: checked it, it could have influenced her future care, for which I am not happy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On our return to Chester, [Baby I] was placed in room 3, which meant in a matter of a week she'd gone from being critically ill on a life support machine to being rushed to Liverpool Women's, to now returning to Chester and being placed in room 3, which is the room before your baby can go home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "But by now our constant attendance at hospital was taking its toll on our one-and-a-half-year-old daughter, so [Father of Baby I] and I decided to split our time. I used to go in 9 am to 3 pm and [Father of Baby I] went 4 pm to 10 pm as he worked during the day. [Baby I] continued to do really well and we were dressing and feeding her."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then recalls an event. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was just changing [Baby I]'s nappy prior to leaving for the day when a nurse called Lucy (at the time I didn't know her surname but now I know it to be Letby) came on duty. It would
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: have been around 3 pm. Lucy came over and said that she thought [Baby I]'s stomach looked swollen, to which I agreed, but [Baby I] appeared okay in herself.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Lucy informed me that she'd keep an eye on her and that she would call for the doctor to also check her out. However, when I got home, I received a call around 4.30 pm. I can't remember from whom but they informed me that [Baby I] had taken bad again. I phoned [Father of Baby I] and told him to get to the hospital. By the time when I arrived, Bernie was resuscitating [Baby I] by conducting chest compressions in room 1 and I was on my own. I can't remember any other members of staff present but there were other staff there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bernie informed me that the swelling to [Baby I]'s stomach had now gone down and that she was doing better. Then the next day, [Baby I] was moved back in room 2. It was a quick change around. But this time we didn't have to change hospitals as [Baby I] had picked up within hours. I'd say [Baby I] was around 6 weeks old at this time, so it would have been mid-September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I also remember [Baby G] had gone poorly loads of times around this time as well, as they were both now back in room 2, and I was trying to reassure [Mother of Baby G] that it would be okay. The nurses were telling me that [Baby I] was doing well again and that it had been known for babies to be sent home from room 2 also.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I noticed that [Baby I] was starting to look differently. She was looking around the room, taking it all in. I was able to sit
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: her on my knee and I remember looking at her and thinking, we're going home. She just looked like a full-term baby. She didn't look frail or small, she just looked like she should be at home in a bed. I started to think she needs to be at home so she doesn't get an infection, as I'd seen so many people not washing their hands and then touching and handling. I just needed her home. I'd send videos home and I was allowed to bathe her, which she loved.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember bathing her for the first time. I was in room 2 and Lucy the nurse was on duty. I was so pleased to be able to bathe her and [Baby I] was obviously enjoying it as she was smiling. Lucy helped prepare the bath and gave advice as to how to bathe her. She even offered to take some photographs using my mobile, to which I agreed. I didn't really have much to do with Lucy. She always appeared reserved compared to some of the nurses. She never really interacted with the parents.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby I] was 8 weeks old, I enquired about her getting her immunisations when she returned home, but the hospital said that they would give them to her while she was in hospital. A female doctor [she doesn't remember the name] prepared us by saying that [Baby I]'s bloods would rise after she'd been immunised, but afterwards Dr Matt told us that [Baby I]'s bloods had risen more than they had expected and that they were going to screen her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was put on antibiotics, but shortly afterwards the female doctor came back in and asked why [Baby I] was on antibiotics. I recall telling her that because of [Baby I]'s history, and because she had declined so rapidly, it was done as a precaution. [Baby I] could go from being perfectly fine to nearly dying within seconds. There was no in between with her. I remember the staff at the hospital kept making a big deal about her stomach swelling.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I also remember at some point, I'm not entirely sure whether it was before or after her immunisation, they tested [Baby I] for cystic fibrosis. I think it was after the immunisation but before she got really sick.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember them asking me to leave the room and when I returned [Baby I] was screaming. I'd never heard her cry so loud. During this time I felt the atmosphere within the hospital had changed. I'd gone from feeling that [Baby I] would be coming home to uncertainty. I remember asking a blonde-haired nurse from room 2 [[Mother of Baby I] doesn't recall that nurse's name] if [Baby I] would likely be going home any time soon, to which she just said, 'We'll see. She comes off her antibiotics on Wednesday so we'll see what they say when she comes off'.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Dave [members of the jury, you've already heard several times from Dr David Harkness and you'll hear a statement from him again in this context] then came and checked [Baby I] and I again asked him how long and he just told me she could wake up tomorrow and not need the heated mattress or it could be 6 months down the line and that's just what it's like for a premature baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was still feeding and was in a heated cot. She was also wired up to monitors. Then this one day we were just sitting there and I remember a nurse called Ashleigh was looking after [Baby I]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, members of the jury, you'll hear from a nurse, Ashleigh Hudson, in relation to the care given to [Baby I]:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember a nurse called Ashleigh was looking after [Baby I]. [Baby G] was with her dad as she had been poorly too. We were all just talking when [Baby I]'s oxygen monitor started bleeping. I turned to Ashleigh and said, 'Is that [Baby I]'s?' to which she replied, 'Yes, it's nothing to worry about, it's just a signal'. Ashleigh then fiddled with the strap, which was attached to [Baby I]'s foot, saying it must be loose, but the bleeping continued. Ashleigh kept reassuring me that everything was okay. However, when I left that night, I didn't feel right. I felt as though it was a start of pattern for [Baby I] as her oxygen and stats levels would always start jumping just before she became poorly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The following morning, I phoned the hospital and spoke with Ashleigh. I asked her if she had sorted the monitor out, to which she informed me that she had actually turned it off, saying [Baby I] didn't need it and for me to stop worrying.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I asked how [Baby I] was, she told me that her temperature had dropped overnight and I remember thinking, that's two signs: first the monitor's bleeping and then her temperature dropping. But Ashleigh kept reassuring me that everything was okay and that she was fine.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Then, later that night, whilst I was at home, we received a call from the hospital, telling us to come immediately. When we arrived, [Baby I] was really poorly. It was the worst she had ever been. The staff had to resuscitate her at least seven or eight times. She just kept flatlining. I remember the following staff being present: Jo, Bernie, Dr Matt, a young nurse who left to go to Australia. Others could have been there, but I can't remember them.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Eventually, they managed to stabilise her. The hospital believed [Baby I] had a bowel problem, but [Baby I] wasn't found
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: this time with a swollen stomach, she was found not breathing. My thoughts were, had they kept the monitors on her, her condition could have been detected earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Over the next few days, [Baby I]'s stomach did swell in the end and she had bruising under her left breastbone. It was blue in colour, a few centimetres in size, which doesn't seem big, but due to [Baby I]'s size it was quite significant.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] continued to be poorly for days and she was continually being resuscitated. The hospital gave us a room to sleep in, but every time we left and started to fall asleep, we'd be woken up with banging on the door telling us to come quickly, and it wasn't once, it was several times every single day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] also seemed to deteriorate when we left her alone and it was predominantly at night. Eventually, Dr Matt said that he was worried. He said that he didn't know if she was going to make it. I recall they phoned Alder Hey to seek advice. Alder Hey said if she stayed on antibiotics for 7 days and stabilised, they'd be able to give her a dye to see what the actual problem is.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Chester were thinking [Baby I] may have had some damage from an earlier NEC, which could have caused damage to the inside of her bowel, which would explain why she'd become poorly as she may have had a build-up in her bowel. I wasn't entirely convinced that this was the cause of [Baby I]'s problems because on this one occasion Ashleigh, the nurse, said that she'd just found her blue in her cot and her stomach hadn't been bloated. I again queried why she had been taken off the oxygen monitor if she had been that poorly as surely this would have picked up the fact that she was having breathing difficulties. I just couldn't understand why they would continue to do that.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "A couple of days later, I felt [Baby I] had picked up, but Belinda, an Australian nurse, pulled me to one side and told me to sit down. She said that [Baby I]'s heart rate, even though it had picked up, was still too low and it had been like that for some time, so she suggested that we get [Baby I] christened. She tried to reassure me that [Baby I] could still get better, but it was something for us to consider.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I felt as though by christening her we were giving up, but we did it. On 15 September 2015 we organised for everyone to come and [Baby I] was christened at the hospital. I think Belinda was there, but I can't remember any other medical staff being present.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Later that day, I was shown a scan of [Baby I]'s lungs. From the scan they looked as though they'd collapsed. Staff at Chester said [Baby I] had to be moved and we were asked where we would like her to go as there was room at Arrowe Park or Liverpool Women's.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Due to Arrowe Park having a McDonald's House, we decided to go there as we would all be able to go as a family. This decision was also made due to the fact that our other daughter [the young daughter] was missing us. However, as [Baby I] was being moved, her stats dropped. I remember Belinda using an implement and sucked loads of fluids out of the lungs before she was placed into a travel incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was then transferred by ambulance to Arrowe Park. When we arrived at Arrowe Park she was X-rayed again and her lungs were fine, they had blown back up, so now I had Arrowe Park telling me that there was nothing wrong with her. I felt as though the staff at Arrowe Park were being rude. They were acting as though they were the better hospital. From what they were telling me, I felt I had to defend the staff at Chester. I told them I'd seen them saving my daughter's life time and time again. But they just kept telling me that [Baby I] was fine and for me to look at her scan.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I tried to tell the nurse and doctor that when she's moved, fluid blocks her lungs, which then stops her breathing, but the doctor just told me that he couldn't understand what I was saying. I understand I may have been upset at the time and not making sense, but he should have listened. A nurse then informed me that she was going to give [Baby I] some milk, to which I said, 'No, she's nil by mouth'. To this, the nurse stopped and apologised and said she'd not read [Baby I]'s notes. I was so angry, I didn't want to be there any longer.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember placing my hand on to [Baby I]'s chest. I could feel her chest bubbling. I told them she wasn't well and there was something going on. I asked the nurse to suction her lungs out because I knew as soon as they moved her, she would drop like a tonne of bricks. But the nurse just kept reassuring me that they had specialist doctors who were looking after [Baby I] and she would be okay.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I again stressed my concerns, saying that [Baby I] was going to crash and again she told me, no, [Baby I]'s lungs are fine. But when the nurse turned [Baby I], she crashed. A doctor then came over waving his arms in the air as though he didn't know what to do, so I screamed at him to get the ventilator, to which he did. [Baby I] then started to pick up and her condition improved.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Looking back now, it always seemed as soon as [Baby I] left Chester Hospital, her condition would improve, but the journey to and from the hospitals would take it out of her, so when I was told she could return back to Chester, I was pleased and happy to return.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was transferred back to Chester by ambulance. The journey was fine and [Baby I] settled back into room 1 on the neonatal ward. I remember going home that night and telling my mum that [Baby I] was awake but she just didn't look herself, it was as though she was looking right through me, as though she couldn't see me.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The staff at the hospital continued to remain positive about [Baby I]'s condition and I started to believe them. Again, I had hope that we would bring her home. That night, we left the hospital at around 22.30 hours. I remember Ashleigh was [Baby I]'s nurse that night, but also present was Lucy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Then at around 00.30 hours I woke up having realised I had slept through a phone call from the hospital. I didn't wait to see if they'd left a message, I just immediately phoned the ward. The phone was answered and I was put on to Ashleigh, who informed me that [Baby I] had just had a little turn and they'd had to put her on a ventilator, but she was okay now.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I put the phone down, I said to [Father of Baby I], 'We've got to go to the hospital'. I wasn't happy with [Baby I] being on the ventilator after all the problems she'd had previously. Loads of thoughts were running through my mind. What if they turned her and it blocked her lungs? I needed to remind them, so I phoned the ward again and someone else answered the reception phone. This person went to find Ashleigh but when they returned they told me that we needed to get to the hospital as soon as we can.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We left home immediately and on our arrival at the hospital we saw Dr Gibbs, Ashleigh and Lucy. They were working to try and resuscitate [Baby I]. I heard them all counting times, so I asked Dr Gibbs how long they'd been doing this to [Baby I], to which he said 20 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I could see every time they were pumping her, her stats would go up, but when they stopped she would flatline every single time. I remember thinking, 'You can't keep doing this to her', and I said to Dr Gibbs, 'You can't do any more'. [Father of Baby I] couldn't watch. I don't know where he went. I think he was in one of the corridors.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whilst they were working on [Baby I], Dr Gibbs gave her an injection. I don't know why or what was in the syringe, but it was given in her leg.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When they eventually stopped working on [Baby I] they passed her to me. She didn't actually die straightaway, it was around 2 am or 3 am in the morning of 23 October when she actually went. I can't be certain as to the exact time as I didn't clock watch as too much was going on.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After she had passed away, we were left alone and all the other babies were moved out of the room, which gave us some privacy. Later on, we were moved to a private room when it became a visiting time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Ashleigh and Lucy asked if I wanted to bathe her. [Father of Baby I] initially said no, but I didn't want to look a back nd regret not doing it, so I said yes. Lucy brought the bath in, saying that if I could get her ready she would come in and take some pictures, which we'd be able to keep. Then whilst [Father of Baby I] and I were bathing her, Lucy came back in. She was smiling and kept going on about how she was present at [Baby I]'s first bath and how much [Baby I] had loved it.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I wish she had just stopped talking. Eventually, I think she realised and stopped. It wasn't something we wanted to hear right then. I just wished she and Ashleigh would go and swap with the next shift. I remember it was Lucy who packaged up [Baby I]'s belongings for us to take home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Prior to leaving the hospital, [Father of Baby I] and I were spoken to by another nurse [she can't recall the name of that nurse] who had blonde hair and Dr Gibbs. Dr Gibbs mentioned about [Baby I] having an autopsy. I said I didn't want her to have one as I just wanted her leaving alone, but he informed me that I didn't have a say and that she needed to have one as her death had been unexpected and the results would be needed to clear the hospital."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She then moves on to [Baby I]'s funeral. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At [Baby I]'s funeral we invited a number of staff members to attend. This included Janet Cox, Jo, Belinda and Dr Matt. However, due to their commitments, only Janet and Jo attended. We did ask for Ashleigh to stay away. I also remember a nurse called Mary also attended."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes the relevant parts of that statement, which, if I remind you again, was dated 20 July 2018.

blocks.text: "I remember Lucy looking over and saying, 'I've noticed her belly is extended today, I'll go and get the doctor to come down to check her'. I remember agreeing with her and thinking that her stomach did look veiny and swollen.

blocks.text: "I was still with [Baby I] when a female doctor came and checked [Baby I] over. She checked [Baby I]'s stomach and said that it seemed soft to touch but they would keep an eye on her. Due to her not showing any concern, I left shortly after 3 pm. I have no recollection of seeing any particular member of staff that day apart from Lucy, as detailed above.

blocks.text: "I was asked if I recalled an incident which occurred on 14 October. This just wouldn't have been possible as there were so many people working on [Baby I]."

Witness statement of DR BALAMURUGAN PALANASAMI (read)
My Lord, may I return to the reading bundle, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And the statement that's paginated at 22 in the top left corner. A statement from a Dr Balamurugan Palanasami dated 5 April 2019. He states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am a consultant neonatologist at the Liverpool Women's Hospital in Liverpool. I started working at that hospital as a consultant in October 2015. [Baby I] was born prematurely at 27 weeks' gestation on 7 August 2015 at 20.47 hours at the Liverpool Women's Hospital, Liverpool. She weighed 970 grams at birth. She was born in very good condition and cried immediately. We assessed her physical condition at birth using the Apgar score. She scored 9 out of 10 at 1 minute and 9 out of 10 at 5 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was received in a plastic bag and was placed on a Transwarmer to keep her warm. Her heart rate was 80 beats per minute, which improved to more than 100 beats per minute immediately after she was given 5 sets of inflation breaths. As routine, she was intubated at 3 minutes of age and she received surfactant medication at 5 minutes of age into her endotracheal tube and she stabilised very well. Her oxygen saturation was 90% in air at 7 minutes of age.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "In summary, she was stabilised very quickly without any major concerns. She was shown to her mum previously and was then admitted into the neonatal intensive care unit at 21.00 hours. I was present at the birth and I was one of the consultants involved in her care on my shifts after her birth until her transfer to Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During pregnancy, [Baby I] was noted to be intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and mum had a prolonged pre-labour rupture of membrane from 26 weeks and she was on antibiotics for almost 1 week prior to [Baby I]'s delivery. Ultrasound dopplers were normal. Mum had two doses of antenatal steroids to help to strengthen her baby's lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] was very stable and didn't require much resuscitation at birth, which was very good. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care at 13 minutes of age. In the unit as a routine practice we inserted umbilical lines. She had a UVC, an umbilical venous catheter, and a UAC, an umbilical arterial catheter. The UVC was not in a good position so it had to be removed and she had a long line inserted. These procedures went smoothly without any problems.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was started on benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, antibiotics, and she was given caffeine, 5 milligrams per kilo. She had vitamin K and nystatin and chlorhexidine powder as per routine unit practice. She was started on the ventilator and she was on minimal breathing support settings on the breathing machine. She stabilised quickly and we were able to wean her ventilation support down quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 8 August 2015, her second day, [Baby I] continued to progress well from weaning with the breathing machine support and she was extubated at 07.00 hours on 8 August 2015. In summary, she was ventilated for 10 hours, which was really good. She was commenced on CPAP of 6 centimetres in 30% oxygen. She again had very good gases post-extubation on this day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her initial bloods that were sent at the time of her birth had come back and showed CRP, which is an infection marker, to be elevated at 42. However, she was already on antibiotics and we had sent a blood culture for her. So we completed our septic screen with a lumbar puncture. She was noted to have jaundice and she was started on single phototherapy. She was commenced on total parenteral nutrition after getting the long line in situ and she continued on this. We commenced her feeds on 8 August 2015 by using maternal expressed breast milk at 0.5ml twohourly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] continued to be stable from a cardiovascular point of view and she had normal blood pressure and didn't require inotropic support. This showed us she was very stable in spite of having an infection.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 9 August 2015, [Baby I] had a cranial ultrasound scan, which was done as a routine, and this came back as normal. She continued to improve very well and she continued to be stable without any concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 12 August 2015, the umbilical arterial catheter was removed. This was used to monitor blood pressure and sampling. It was removed because it was no longer needed. She continued to have her long line in situ for her total parenteral nutrition and her feeds continued to be increased.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 3 August 2015, [Baby I] was noted to have an increased temperature and she had increased desaturations and bradycardia and her HeRO score, which is one of the scores we use to monitor for infection, was elevated as well. She was re-screened, which included also sending a full blood count, CRP and blood culture, and we started [Baby I] on a second line of antibiotics, which were co-amoxicillin and gentamicin.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The CRP infection marker came back as less than 4. However, her white cell count was elevated at 45.4 times 106/1, so we decided to give 5 days' antibiotics. During this episode her feeds were briefly stopped. However, they were restarted later that evening on 13 August 2015 and she continued to tolerate those feeds without any concerns. She had two-hourly blood pressure monitoring during this episode. She continued to have normal blood pressure and didn't require any inotropic support. She managed to have some time off from CPAP, the respiratory support, which showed she was stable from a respiratory point of view.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] completed 5 days' of antibiotics from 13 August 2015, mainly for the elevated white cell count. Her highest white cell count was on 15 August 2015, which was 51.4 times 106/1. However, it continued to decrease.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 17 August 2015, her white cell count was 28.8 times 106/1. She continued to have time off from CPAP. We continued to build on the time off and we continued to increase the milk feeds daily as per our protocol. She continued to improve and stabilise. There was no rise in CRP during this episode. She had a lumbar puncture done which came back as normal without any signs of meningitis. Her blood culture was negative at 36 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 18 August 2015 she was stable on CPAP and she had 4 hours off from CPAP. She was on a pressure of 5 centimetres of water and between 24% and 28% of oxygen. She was on a total of 165ml per kilogram per day of total fluids and she was on 5.5ml twohourly of expressed breast milk. She was tolerating the feeds very well. She was having regular bowel opening and she was passing urine well. She had normal tone, posture and movement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The CRP remained less than 4 and her HeRO score remained low at less than 4. She had already completed 5 days of antibiotics for raised white cell count. She was set with an incubator humidity of 50%, which is expected for her gestational age. She was considered to be ready to go back to Chester Hospital for further care, so we contacted the Chester team in the morning and we arranged for her transfer to Chester. We had to wait for a bed space to become available before she was moved to Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When she went to Chester she was on the following medication: caffeine, nystatin and chlorhexidine, which is routine and expected at that stage of her life.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was transferred on day 11 and weighed 1,060 grams, which was 90 grams above her birth weight. This was good as we normally expect babies to reach their birth weight after a drop around day 10 of life.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During her first stay at Liverpool Women's Hospital our concern was the infection which was treated with antibiotics. We expected [Baby I] to continue to improve at Chester with no ongoing concerns."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: He then produces some documents, the handwritten medical notes for [Baby I]'s first period of stay at the Liverpool Women's Hospital between the 17th and 18 August.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Then he turns to [Baby I]'s return to the Liverpool Women's Hospital:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The second period of stay for [Baby I] was when she came back to us at the Liverpool Women's Hospital on 6 September 2015. She was admitted at 15.41 hours. She was a post-natal transfer from Chester. The diagnosis we were given was suspected necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The information we were given during admission was that she was self-ventilating in air in Chester and was fully fed. She was tolerating milk at 180ml per kilogram per day until 5 September 2015. [Baby I] started to have an increase in desaturations and bradycardia on 5 September 2015. She was intubated and ventilated and she was started on antibiotics at Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "They were also concerned about her abdomen, which was distended and full. She had an abdominal X-ray performed in Chester, which showed dilated bowel loops with thickened bowel wall, and they were concerned about necrotising enterocolitis. They expected a surgical review and assessment, this being the main reason they transferred [Baby I] to the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On arrival to the Liverpool Women's Hospital, she was on a ventilator, was on a pressure setting of 20/5 and a rate of 60 in air. She had good tidal volumes and her blood gases were normal. On examination, she had a normal heart rate and her capillary refill, which is a marker of tissue perfusion, was 2 to 3 seconds centrally and peripherally. Her lactate was 1, which again showed a normal tissue perfusion.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Dewhurst was the on-call consultant on that day. He examined [Baby I] on arrival. We discussed with Mr Simon Kenny, who was
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: the surgical consultant on call at Alder Hey Children's Hospital. Having gone through all her background and her current condition it was decided that she did not need a surgical review at that time and they were thinking that she had sepsis rather than necrotising enterocolitis. However, it was decided to continue on triple antibiotics, so she was changed to amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole to cover for necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] continued to be stable. She was kept nil by mouth on 6 September 2015. She had a stable night on 6 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 7 September, in the morning at 07.00 hours, she blocked her endotracheal tube because of thick secretions. It was a mechanical obstruction. The medical team were unable to move the chest with inflation breaths. Her saturations failed to improve, so she was re-intubated immediately with a 3 size [which should be size 3, I imagine] endotracheal tube, which was fixed at 7 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After this, she had normal gases and she improved very well. She continued to show clinical improvement and her ventilator support was gradually weaned. She was extubated on 8 September 2015 at 10.00 hours to incubator/oxygen. She continued to selfventilate, needing minimal oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her total duration of ventilation at the Liverpool Women's Hospital was less than 48 hours. Her abdomen continued to improve and she no longer had abdominal distension. Her feeds were started on 7 September 2015 at 0.5ml two-hourly. She tolerated her feed very well for 24 hours. Her feed volume was then increased to 1ml on 8 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Because of the concern about necrotising enterocolitis, the plan was to cautiously increase the feeding volume and follow a cautious feeding regimen. Instead of the standard regimen of 0.5ml twelve-hourly, she was increased to 1ml every 24 hours. The plan was to complete a five-day course of antibiotics involving co-amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole. She had a long line in situ.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "However, on 9 September 2015, the long line was found to be tracking with a redness mark on the skin, meaning it was getting infected. Her CRP, which had decreased to 5.6, increased to 34.4 on 9 September, so her long line was removed and she was changed to teicoplanin, gentamicin and metronidazole.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She had a repeat of her blood culture. After the change of antibiotic, her infection marker continued to decrease and all the antibiotics were finally stopped on 11 September 2009 (sic) having had a full five-day course of antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During her stay, a routine swab screening was done on 10 September 2015. This showed that she was colonised with staphylococcus aureus and stenotrophomonas maltophilia organisms. These were new colonisations which were not -- we were not aware of before. However, she was clinically improving very well when we received the swab alert results. She had completed a good period of antibiotics with normal CRP, she continued to self-ventilate in air, and she continued to tolerate her feeds and we were able to increase her feeds as well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "To clarify, in relation to the swab alert, normally babies will not have any organisms in their body. We consider them sterile when they are born. If they have anything in their body it means they've got it from their incubator, environment, mother or people handling them. So we normally do weekly swabs, especially when babies are transferred from another hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We do these swabs to guide us during the antibiotic selection when they deteriorate, whether we need to use our standard line of antibiotics or if we need to use special antibiotics to start targeting the colonising organism. It's also mainly for our information so that we can isolate such babies for special precautions as well as care for them in hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 13 September 2015, having spent nearly 6 days in the Liverpool Women's Hospital, [Baby I] proved to us that she continued to be stable and this infection episode had been complicated by the line tracking, which improved very well without any major effect on her. She was self-ventilating in air and she had occasional self-correcting desaturations, which were recorded twice in the preceding 24 hours. She was on regular caffeine, which was normal for her corrected gestational age. She was on 150ml per kilogram per day of total fluids and she was having 6ml of expressed milk two-hourly via the nasogastric tube with no vomits. She was passing urine. Her abdomen continued to be very soft. She last opened her bowels on 8 September 2015. However, she was kept nil by mouth for some time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her abdomen was soft, so we were reassured. She was on onethird enteral feeds and two-thirds total parenteral nutrition. Her new long line was in situ for 5 days, her CRP was 4, and she had normal neurology and cardiology examinations, so she was stable enough to transfer back to Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "To clarify on the self-correcting desaturations on 13 September 2015, babies who self-ventilate in air at extreme preterm, which [Baby I] was at 27 weeks, sometimes their saturations might drop because when they move. The saturation probe might not pick up
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: the signals, so they drop briefly. It sometimes comes back without us needing to do anything.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The main concern with premature babies is that if they stop breathing because the brain respiratory centres are not mature enough to stimulate them to breathe all the time. This is why we start them on caffeine.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "If the desaturations last for a longer period of time they then become bradycardic. Then we might need to do interventions such as bagging and breathing for them, stimulating them. If babies don't require stimulating or bagging, this is reassuring so we don't worry about self-correcting desaturations as this is more likely to be caused by movement or placement of probes on the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When [Baby I] initially came to us, the abdominal X-ray showed dilated bowel loops with a thickened bowel wall, but that quickly settled down. We had attributed this to probably infection related or poor gut motility. So we were not convinced that this was necrotising enterocolitis, NEC, as the rest of the markers for NEC were normal. Her lactate was normal. The full blood count was normal with normal platelets and there was no acidosis. She didn't have significant gastric aspirates.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We started her feeds the very next day on 7 September 2015. Normally, if we are worried about necrotising enterocolitis, we keep them nil by mouth for at least 5 days until we finish the antibiotics. As we were not convinced it was necrotising enterocolitis, we decided to start feeds after 24 hours. We were proved to be correct on this decision as she continued to tolerate feeds and we were able to build up feeds regularly to 6ml every 2 hours in 5 days.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 13 September 2015, [Baby I] was well enough to return to the Countess of Chester Hospital and our expectations were that she would continue to improve and there were no ongoing concerns."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, in the next paragraph, as you will see, he simply produces, effectively, exhibits, her medical records, from which this narrative has been drawn.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He does that in part in the first part of the next paragraph when he produces a biochemistry chart and then he states:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This chart shows the infection marker, CRP, is elevated at birth and shows, after the first period of antibiotics for 5 days, a reduction in her infection marker to less than 4. Due to
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: her white cell count being elevated to 51.5 she had another period of antibiotics during her first period of stay with us at the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On the second period of stay, which was on 6 September 2015, this chart shows [Baby I]'s CRP marker was 5.9, which elevated to 34.4. blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER
